records.question: What is asthma?
records.answer: Asthma is a common condition that affects the airways in and out of your lungs. These airways can become sensitive and inflamed, making it harder to breathe and causing symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, shortness of breath, and chest tightness. Because the airways are so sensitive, certain things can trigger the muscles around the airways to tighten. This makes the airways narrower. The airway lining also becomes inflamed, causing the further narrowing of the airways and increased sputum production. (section: what-is-asthma)

records.question: Which inhaler do I need to take every day?
records.answer: The Preventer inhaler needs to be taken every day even if you are symptom free. (section: treatment)

records.question: My mouth gets sore after using my inhaler. What can I do about it?
records.answer: Rinse your mouth after use to reduce the chance of soreness. (section: treatment)

records.question: What are the common triggers for asthma symptoms?
records.answer: Common triggers for asthma symptoms include: • Colds and viruses • Allergies – e.g. animal hair, pollen • Dust / Pollution / Smoke • Stress or heightened emotions • Temperature extremes / temperature change • Hormones • Strong smells – e.g. perfumes, aerosols, cleaning products (section: triggers)

records.question: How is asthma diagnosed?
records.answer: There is no one test to diagnose asthma. A diagnosis is made based on your symptom history and the results of breathing tests. (section: how-diagnosed)

records.question: Can exercise bring on my asthma symptoms?
records.answer: Yes, exercise can bring on asthma symptoms in some people. (section: triggers)

records.question: Where can I find more reliable information about asthma?
records.answer: The Asthma and Lung UK website is an excellent source of reliable information. https://www.asthma.org.uk/ (section: further-info)

records.question: How do I get this leaflet in Braille or large print?
records.answer: To get this leaflet in Braille or large print, contact the Patient Advice and Liaison Service (PALS): • 01752 439694 • Plh-tr.PALS@nhs.net (section: further-info)

records.question: What is the maximum number of puffs of my reliever inhaler during an asthma attack?
records.answer: The maximum number of puffs of your reliever inhaler during an asthma attack is 10 puffs. (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: During an attack, how often should I take a puff?
records.answer: During an asthma attack, you should take one puff of your reliever inhaler every 30-60 seconds, up to a maximum of 10 puffs. (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: How many times a week can I use my reliever and still count as well controlled?
records.answer: Your asthma is considered well controlled if you do not require your reliever inhaler more than 3 times per week. (section: well-controlled)

records.question: What proportion of people with asthma have severe asthma?
records.answer: Around 5% of all people with asthma have a diagnosis of severe asthma. (section: is-it-serious)

records.question: While waiting for the ambulance, how long should I wait before repeating the puffs?
records.answer: While waiting for the ambulance, you should wait **15 minutes** before repeating the puffs. (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: I keep waking up at night with a tight chest. Does that mean my treatment is working?
records.answer:
Waking at night with asthma symptoms, such as a tight chest, is not a sign that your treatment is working. Instead, it is a sign that your asthma may not be well-controlled. (section: well-controlled) 

If you are experiencing this, it is important to seek medical advice to review and adjust your treatment plan. (section: treatment)

records.question: Does this run in families?
records.answer: Yes, asthma can run in families. This is thought to be due to both genetics and the living environment you live and grow up in. (section: why-people-get-asthma)

records.question: Will I ever be completely free of this?
records.answer: Asthma is a generally lifelong condition. Whilst there is no cure for asthma, there are very effective treatments and most people who have asthma can be symptom free most of the time. (section: treatment)

records.question: I feel completely fine at the moment. Can I stop taking my steroid inhaler?
records.answer: The documents state that preventer inhalers need to be taken every day even if you are symptom-free (section: treatment). Stopping medication without medical advice may compromise asthma control. Always consult your healthcare provider before adjusting treatment. (section: treatment)

records.question: I've been getting a tight chest and a whistling sound when I breathe at night. Is that asthma?
records.answer: The documents describe symptoms like chest tightness and wheezing (whistling sound when breathing) as possible signs of asthma or an asthma attack. However, they do not confirm that these specific symptoms alone diagnose asthma. For a proper assessment, consult a healthcare professional. (section: what-is-asthma, section: asthma-attack)

records.question: My son was born six weeks early. Does that make asthma more likely for him?
records.answer: Yes, being born prematurely is considered a risk factor for asthma. (section: why-people-get-asthma)

records.question: My job is really dusty and I've started wheezing. Could the two be connected?
records.answer: The documents mention that occupational exposure to substances like dust can lead to asthma in some individuals (section: why-people-get-asthma). Wheezing is a symptom of asthma (section: what-is-asthma). While the documents do not explicitly state that dust directly causes wheezing in this scenario, occupational exposure is listed as a risk factor for asthma. For personalized advice, consult a healthcare professional. (section: why-people-get-asthma, section: what-is-asthma)

records.question: I'm going through the menopause and I've suddenly become breathless. Is that related?
records.answer: The documents mention that hormonal changes, including those during menopause, can be a risk factor for asthma (section: why-people-get-asthma). However, they do not explicitly state that menopause directly causes breathlessness. Sudden breathlessness could be a symptom of an asthma attack or other conditions. For personalized advice, consult a healthcare professional. (section: why-people-get-asthma, section: asthma-attack)

records.question: I use my reliever about five times a week and I had an attack last month. What should I do?
records.answer:
Your asthma is not well controlled, as using a reliever inhaler more than 3 times per week and experiencing a recent attack are signs of poorly controlled asthma (section: well-controlled). You should consult your healthcare provider to review your treatment plan, as additional therapies may be needed (section: treatment). Do not delay seeking medical advice.  

(section: well-controlled, section: treatment)

records.question: List, in order, everything I should do the moment an asthma attack starts.
records.answer:
• Sit up straight – don’t lie down. Try to keep calm  
• Take one puff of your reliever inhaler every 30-60 seconds up to a maximum of 10 puffs  
• If you feel worse at any point or don’t feel better after 10 puffs, call 999 for an ambulance  
• Repeat step 2 after 15 minutes while you are waiting for an ambulance (section: asthma-attack)

records.question: Why might someone only develop asthma as an adult rather than as a child?
records.answer: Someone might develop asthma as an adult due to factors such as: • Occupational exposure to certain substances such as dust or chemicals. • Hormones – some women develop late-onset asthma during or after the menopause. (section: why-people-get-asthma)

records.question: I'm having an asthma attack right now. What do I do?
records.answer:
• Sit up straight – don’t lie down. Try to keep calm  
• Take one puff of your reliever inhaler every 30-60 seconds up to a maximum of 10 puffs  
• If you feel worse at any point or don’t feel better after 10 puffs, call 999 for an ambulance

records.question: I've taken 10 puffs and I don't feel better. Can I just take 5 more?
records.answer: If you've taken 10 puffs and still don’t feel better, call 999 for an ambulance immediately. While waiting, repeat step 2 (take one puff every 30–60 seconds) as instructed. Do not exceed the recommended steps without medical guidance. (section: asthma-attack)
